units.title: Ethereum mainnet reference and cross-chain deployment parity
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 16 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Leads L-800 and L-801. research/network-risk/cycles/016/theme-monad-harness-exact.work holds a harness on the exact dependencies of category-labs/monad v0.16.7 and v0.16.5 (harness.cpp, replay.cpp, build.sh, link.sh, the instrumented emitter under shapes/ with pm.marks and the assembly logs, the micro programs under micro/, task4.json with the shape of every site). It runs the deployed PoolManager code interpreted and native from one state and compares results, gas, storage, transient storage and logs. Four sites of the native code had their exact register or stack arm executed by no PoolManager scenario: CALLDATALOAD at pc 12232, MULMOD with constant modulus 2^128 at pc 22378 (src/libraries/FullMath.sol:47-49), SAR at pc 15519 (BalanceDelta.amount0, src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:62-64) and SHL at pc 16642. A fault planted at the other constant-modulus site (pc 22639, modulus 2^96) changed no PoolManager result. Task 1: for each of the five sites, read from the instrumented assembly log the exact arm the PoolManager's own block uses (operand locations, registers, stack offsets) and build a test that executes the PoolManager's own block at that pc, not a micro program of the same coarse shape. Two ways are acceptable: PoolManager calls whose inputs reach the pc (find them by solving the path from jumpmap.json and the source), or a harness entry that starts the native code of the deployed runtime at the enclosing basic block with a prepared stack and memory. Say which you used and prove the site ran (marker count). Task 2, FullMath: read src/libraries/FullMath.sol:14-54 and :58-70. At the remainder sites the code computes remainder := mulmod(a, b, denominator), then prod1 := sub(prod1, gt(remainder, prod0)) and prod0 := sub(prod0, remainder). Name every caller that passes a constant denominator (FixedPoint96.Q96, FixedPoint128.Q128) and which of the two pcs each compiles to. Drive both sites with operands where the 512 bit product has prod1 equal to 1 and prod0 equal to 0, 1, 2^96 - 1, 2^96, 2^128 - 1, 2^128 and values just below and above the modulus, and where prod1 is the largest value the require allows. Compare native and interpreted results word for word, and compare both with Python integers. Then answer from the source: if the native remainder were wrong at such an input, could the result drop below 2^160 and be accepted by src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:68 or :90, by the casts of src/libraries/Pool.sol, or by the fee growth accounting of Position.update and Pool.modifyLiquidity? Which ordinary call (swap, modifyLiquidity, donate) reaches each site with prod1 equal to 1, and with which pool state? Task 3, BalanceDelta: build PoolManager scenarios (swap, modifyLiquidity, donate) whose returned delta has amount0 equal to -1, -2^127, 2^127 - 1 and 0 and amount1 with the top bit set, and others with the two halves swapped; run them interpreted and native on both releases and compare. Report the marker count of pc 15519 and pc 16642. Task 4: plant a fault at each of the five exact sites (one at a time) and show that your tests fail. A site whose fault no test catches is a result to report as such. A difference between native and interpreted code on any input an ordinary account can supply is a finding with actor unprivileged on chain 143; say whether it moves funds.

Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Leads L-810 and L-802. Every script comparison so far (tools/opdiff/pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, pmdiff6.py and their inputs in research/network-risk/opcodes/) placed the PoolManager bytecode at a fresh address by state override, with its immutable rewritten. Rules that a node keys on the real PoolManager address, on existing storage or on how often a contract runs never applied to those runs: Arc's value-call frame hook, Avalanche's storage key fold on existing slots (F-040), Tempo's transfer policies, MegaETH's per-account accounting, any compile or cache decision keyed by code hash, address or use count. The PoolManager addresses and endpoints are in research/network-risk/state/networks.json. Task 1: write a driver that runs the same script sets against the real PoolManager address of each of the 21 networks with code and storage left as on chain. Only the driver contract (the unlock callback, token doubles and hook doubles) is injected by state override, and the scripts create their own pools with fresh keys so existing pools are not needed; where a script needs token balances, override the doubles, never the PoolManager. Run sets 1, 2 and 6 and compare every returned word with the Ethereum run at Ethereum's real address and with the fresh-address results already stored. Explain every difference (gas limits, base fee, block context); a difference in a returned amount, a delta, a slot or a revert reason that the explanation does not cover is a finding. Task 2: run research/network-risk/cycles/016/arbitrum-family.work/offsets.py (CALLDATALOAD, CALLDATACOPY, RETURNDATACOPY, MCOPY, CODECOPY and KECCAK256 with offsets from 2^31 to 2^256-1, zero lengths at large offsets, return data copies whose offset plus length overflows) on the 18 networks where it has not run, and report any word that differs from the three Arbitrum chains and from the specification. Pay attention to the Go clients (bor on Polygon, BNB Chain geth, coreth on Avalanche, the op-geth backend of Celo) and to Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM. Task 3: at the real address, read through extsload and exttload the slots the source defines (src/PoolManager.sol, src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol, Lock.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol) inside and after a simulated unlock on each network and confirm that the unlock flag, the delta count and the synced currency read zero at the start of a call, so no state of an earlier transaction of the same block is visible to a simulated one. Report per network.

The reference interpreter tools/opdiff/pyevm.py judged many earlier comparisons. Cycle 16 found that it gave a DELEGATECALL frame a call value of zero; the shared file was fixed on 2026-11-25 (call() takes apparent=). The PoolManager contains no DELEGATECALL, so comparisons limited to PoolManager frames stand, but replays of whole transactions through routers may have matched or failed for the wrong reason. Task 1: audit pyevm.py opcode by opcode against the Ethereum execution specification for Cancun (and Prague where a network runs it): every opcode it implements, gas-independent semantics only. Check in particular CALL with value to a non-existent account, value transfer and balance checks, STATICCALL write protection through nested frames, RETURNDATASIZE and RETURNDATACOPY after each kind of call and after a failed call, CALLCODE if present, SELFBALANCE, EXTCODESIZE and EXTCODEHASH of empty and delegated accounts, MCOPY overlap, memory expansion on zero-length operations, transient storage across DELEGATECALL (keyed by the storage address), snapshot and restore of storage, transient storage, balances and logs on every failure path, precompiles 1 to 10, and the signed arithmetic helpers. Write a test file that runs each case and compare with a second source of truth: eth_call with state overrides on https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com for the same bytecode. Report each fault with the line. Task 2: list every script under research/network-risk/tools and research/network-risk/cycles/*/ *.work that imports pyevm.py or a copy of it (pyevm2.py, pyevm_tx.py), and for each say whether it ran frames other than the PoolManager and whether any fault from Task 1 could change its outcome. Rerun the affected ones that can still be rerun (block-level removal simulators of cycles 11 and 12, the mined-branch replays of cycle 13, the whole-transaction reruns of cycle 16) with the fixed interpreter, and report every outcome that changes. Task 3: extend cycles/016/theme-revert-rollback-mined.work/pyevm_tx.py with models of the node-implemented contracts it stopped at (TIP-20 tokens on Tempo from the tempo v1.19.1 source in /home/user/tempoxyz/tempo, B20 tokens on Base, ArbGasInfo and ArbSys on the Nitro chains) and rerun the reverted-then-completed unlock transactions it could not run, starting with Tempo 0xba5c0224452fbe54eb5198aad0bba1cf5a4b86db6e40eb4f4265024a79bdfa27 and Arbitrum One 0x33050352c9e5c462c3f86d454679d163a822785ba932ba6b8f3dae35c12dfd4b (use an archive endpoint for the parent state). A PoolManager frame or slot that ends differently on the chain and in the reference is a finding.

Task 1, HyperEVM: the public replay clients of HyperEVM pin ruint 1.15.0 (hyper-evm-sync) and 1.16.0 (nanoreth), both inside advisory RUSTSEC-2025-0137 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rustsec/advisory-db/main/crates/ruint/RUSTSEC-2025-0137.md): algorithms::div::reciprocal_mg10 relies on debug_assert and can read out of bounds in release builds. Download both ruint versions from crates.io into your work directory, find every caller of reciprocal_mg10, and say whether each caller normalises the divisor before the call on the paths the revm versions of those clients use for DIV, MOD, SDIV, SMOD, ADDMOD and MULMOD. Then build a small Rust program against each ruint version in release mode and run the division and modular vectors of research/network-risk/opcodes (battery and targeted sets, and the 8,908 mulDiv vectors named in OPCODES.md) through div_rem, add_mod and mul_mod exactly as the revm handlers call them; compare with Python integers. Report any wrong word and whether FullMath, SqrtPriceMath or SwapMath can produce its operands. Task 2, reth cache: F-133 and F-132 (state/findings.json) rest on one link: a read that puts a storage word of an address without code into the reth execution cache before a block destroys and recreates it. Cycle 16 read revm 42.0.0 (OP Mainnet, Base, Zora, World Chain) and found no default path that makes that read. Do the same reading for celo-reth (revm-interpreter 35.0.1 from celo-org/revm), X Layer reth v0.0.7 (revm-interpreter 37.0.3) and reth-bsc: does State::storage or its equivalent answer storage of an account created, not existing or destroyed in the block without a database read? Is there a default path that caches a storage word of a codeless address? Then say whether a block builder with the cache flag on takes any path the default does not, and give one consistent rating for F-132 and F-133 with the reason. Task 3, MegaETH: the stateless validator built in research/network-risk/cycles/016/theme-megaeth-validator-build.work/build (binary target/release/stateless-validator, run notes in the research file of that unit) validated 43,645 blocks chosen by PoolManager logs up to block 32,766,000, with the pre-state anchored to the parent root on 45 of them. Find the blocks that hold a transaction to or through the PoolManager without a PoolManager log (native settle, sync, clear, reverted unlocks; use eth_getBlockReceipts and callTracer) and the blocks after 32,766,000 with PoolManager activity, run the validator on them, and run at least 2,000 blocks in the mode that anchors the pre-state to the parent root. Report every block that fails and why. Task 4, Go clients: Elysium's node is built with go1.25.12, which lacks two amd64 compiler fixes (F-136). Which Go release builds the bor, BNB Chain geth, avalanchego and celo op-geth binaries that the endpoints report (release notes, Dockerfiles, CI files at the release tags), and does any of them fall in the affected range of Go issues 79874 and 80517? If one does, run cycles/016/arbitrum-family.work/offsets.py on that network.
